summary: This document defines ways to identify a digital object using the output of a hash function. It specifies a new URI scheme, a way to map such names to HTTP URLs, and binary and human-speakable formats. The names can link strongly to the content, so the object can be checked against its reference.

plainLanguage.summary: A name built from a fingerprint of a file can also prove the file is the right one. The problem was that everyone was writing those names in a different way. This document sets down one standard way to write them, in five formats.

questions: how to name things with hashes
what is the ni uri scheme
how to name a file by its hash
subtitle: Standard ways to name a digital object by the fingerprint of its bytes, so the name can prove the object is right.

tldr.problem: Deployments put hash outputs into their identifiers in their own ways, which causes interoperability problems, and there was no standard way to check that a retrieved object matches the name used to request it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the ni URI scheme, a mapping to .well-known HTTP(S) URLs, a URL segment form, a compact binary format and a human-speakable nih URI scheme, all built from an algorithm name and a hash value.
tldr.outcome: A name can carry a strong link to its object, so the object can be authenticated to the same degree as the reference to it. sha-256 is mandatory to implement.

today: RFC 6920 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2013, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The 'ni' and 'nih' URI schemes and the 'ni' well-known URI are registered as permanent.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Identifiers, that is, names or locators, are used in various protocols to identify resources. In many scenarios those identifiers contain values obtained from hash functions, and different deployments have chosen different ways to include the hash function output in their identifiers. The result is interoperability problems.

This document defines the Named Information identifier, which provides a set of standard ways to use hash function outputs in names. It also defines a new URI scheme, a mapping to HTTP URLs, and binary and human-speakable formats for these names. The formats are designed to support, but not require, a strong link to the referenced object, so that the object may be authenticated to the same degree as the reference to it. The stated reason for the work is to standardise current uses of hash outputs in URLs and to support new information-centric applications and other uses of hash outputs in protocols.

Hash function outputs are used in several ways: to ensure uniqueness when mapping URIs to a specific resource, to make URIs hard to guess for security reasons, and to verify that a resource representation obtained over the network really corresponds to the name that was used to request it, which this document calls name-data integrity. Other applications include creating references from web pages delivered over HTTP/TLS, DNS resource records signed using DNSSEC, and data values embedded in certificates or Certificate Revocation Lists.

Not all uses of these names require the full hash output. Truncated hashes can be safely used in some environments, so the document defines a new IANA registry of hash functions for use with these names, so that strong and weak, truncated, algorithms are not mixed in other protocol registries.
sections.plainLanguage: A name built from a fingerprint of a file can also prove the file is the right one. The problem was that everyone was writing those names differently, so this document sets down one standard way to write them.

sections.title: Hashes Are What Count
sections.content:
When comparing two names of the form defined here, an implementation MUST consider only the digest algorithm and the digest value. It MUST NOT consider other fields, such as an authority field from a URI or any parameters. Two hashes are identical, regardless of encoding, if the decoded hashes are based on the same algorithm and have the same length and the same binary value. In that case the two names can be treated as referring to the same thing.

The sha-256 algorithm is mandatory to implement, so implementations MUST be able to generate, send, accept and process names based on a sha-256 hash. Implementations MAY support additional hash algorithms and MAY use them for specific names, for example in a constrained environment where sha-256 is not optimal, or where truncated names are needed to fit into the corresponding protocols and a higher collision probability can be tolerated.

Truncated hashes MAY be supported, and when a hash value is truncated the name MUST indicate this. Different hash algorithm strings are used for that, such as sha-256-32 for a 32-bit truncation of a sha-256 output. A 32-bit truncated hash is essentially useless for security in almost all cases but might be useful for naming. With current best practices, very few, if any, applications making use of names with less than 100-bit hashes will have useful security properties.

When a hash value is truncated to N bits, the leftmost N bits, that is, the most significant N bits in network byte order, MUST be used as the truncated value. The document gives the example of a 128-bit hash output 0x265357902fe1b7e2a04b897c6025d7a2 truncated to 32 bits, giving 0x26535790.

When the input to the hash algorithm is a public key value, as may be used by various security protocols, the hash SHOULD be calculated over the public key in an X.509 SubjectPublicKeyInfo structure. That input was chosen primarily for compatibility with the DANE TLSA protocol, but it also includes any relevant public key parameters in the hash input, which is sometimes necessary for security reasons. It does not force the use of X.509 or full compliance with the certificate profile, since formatting any public key as a SubjectPublicKeyInfo is relatively straightforward and well supported by libraries. Other than in this special case, the document does not specify the hash function input; other specifications are expected to define it.
sections.plainLanguage: Two names are the same only if they use the same hash, the same length and the same value. Everything else, such as the host part, is ignored. A shortened hash is a different name, not a shorter way of writing the same one.

sections.title: The ni URI Format
sections.content:
A Named Information URI consists of nine components. The scheme name is 'ni'. It is followed by the literal characters '://'. The authority is optional and may help applications access the object named by the URI; there is no default value for it. While ni names with and without an authority differ syntactically from ni names with different authorities, all three refer to the same object if and only if the digest algorithm, length and value are the same. A single '/' follows the authority. The digest algorithm is the name of the algorithm, as specified in the IANA registry. The literal ';' separates it from the digest value, which MUST be encoded using base64url with no '=' padding characters. The '?' separates the digest value from the query parameters, a 'tag=value' list as used with HTTP URLs, with a '&' between each. For compatibility with Internationalized Resource Identifiers, non-ASCII characters in the query part MUST be encoded as UTF-8 and the resulting octets MUST be percent-encoded.

It is OPTIONAL for implementations to check the integrity of the URI and resource mapping when sending, receiving or processing ni URIs. Escaping follows the rules of RFC 3986, so percent-encoding distinguishes between the reserved and unreserved functions of the same character in the same URI component. For example, an ampersand separates attribute-value pairs in the query part, so an ampersand inside a value has to be escaped as '%26'. A slash has no reserved function in a query part and does not have to be escaped, though it can still appear escaped as '%2f' or '%2F', and implementations have to be able to understand such escaped forms.

The 'val' field MUST contain the output of base64url encoding, without '=' padding, of the result of applying the hash function 'alg' to its defined input, which defaults to the object bytes expected to be returned when the URI is dereferenced. Relative ni URIs can occur, and the algorithm in Section 5 of RFC 3986 applies to them.

The Content Type query string attribute, 'ct', specifies the MIME Content Type of the associated data. Implementations MUST support parsing the 'ct=' attribute name. Protocols that use ni URIs need to specify how to verify name-data integrity for the content types they process, and should take into account possible Content-Transfer-Encodings. Implementations SHOULD support name-data integrity validation for at least the application/octet-stream Content Type with no explicit Content-Transfer-Encoding. The hash is calculated after the Content-Transfer-Encoding is removed, so it applies to the raw data. If the user agent is sensitive to the content type, the ni name carries a 'ct=' attribute, and the object is retrieved over a protocol that specifies a Content Type, and the two content types do not match, then the client SHOULD handle that as a potential security error.
sections.plainLanguage: An ni URI has a fixed shape: the letters 'ni', then the name of the hash, then a semicolon, then the hash value written in a URL-safe base64 form. An optional host name may follow 'ni://' and a query string may follow a question mark.

sections.title: The .well-known HTTP Mapping
sections.content:
The document defines a mapping between ni URIs and HTTP or HTTPS URLs that makes use of the .well-known URI mechanism by defining an 'ni' suffix. The HTTP(S) mapping MAY be used in any context where clients with support for ni URIs are not available. Because the .well-known name space is not intended for general information retrieval, a client that dereferences a .well-known/ni URL over HTTP(S) will often receive a 3xx redirection response, and a client sending such a request MUST be able to handle that.

For an ni name of the form 'ni://n-authority/alg;val?query-string', the corresponding HTTP(S) URL is 'http://h-authority/.well-known/ni/alg/val?query-string'. If the ni name has a specified authority, the h-authority MUST have the same value. If the ni name has no authority, an h-authority value MAY be derived from the application context, for example the origin of the web site being viewed. In general there are no guarantees that the object named by the ni URI is available at the corresponding HTTP(S) URL, but if any data is returned, the retriever can determine whether or not it is content that matches the ni URI.

In the other direction, an application presented with an HTTP(S) URL whose pathname starts with '/.well-known/ni/' may be able to derive a meaningful ni URI, but there is no guarantee of that. When mapping from an ni URI to a .well-known URL, an implementation has to decide between an 'http' and an 'https' URL. If the object referenced does in fact match the hash in the URL, there is arguably no need for additional data integrity when the ni URI or .well-known URL was received securely, but TLS also provides confidentiality, so there can still be reasons to use 'https', and web server policy such as HTTP Strict Transport Security may dictate that data is only available over 'https'.
sections.plainLanguage: If a server cannot speak ni URIs, the same name can be turned into a normal web address under '/.well-known/ni/'. The server usually answers with a redirect to the real location.

sections.title: The URL Segment Format
sections.content: Some applications may benefit from using hashes in existing HTTP URLs or other URLs. To do this, one simply uses the 'alg-val' production from the ni name scheme ABNF, which may be included, for example, in the pathname, query string or even fragment components of HTTP URLs. In such cases there is nothing present in the URL that ensures that a client can depend on this specification, so clients MUST NOT assume that any URL with a pathname component that matches the 'alg-val' production was in fact produced as a result of this specification. That URL might or might not be related to this specification; only the context will tell.
sections.plainLanguage: The same 'algorithm;value' pair can be dropped into an ordinary web address. Nothing in the address says it came from this specification, so software must not assume it did.

sections.title: The Binary Format
sections.content: If a more space-efficient version of the name is needed, a binary format can be used. It consists of two fields: a header and the hash value. The header field defines how the identifier has been created, and the hash value holds a possibly truncated result of a one-way hash over whatever is being identified. The Res field is a reserved 2-bit field for future use, and it MUST be set to zero for this specification and ignored on receipt. The hash algorithm and truncation length are specified by the Suite ID. For maintaining efficient encoding for the binary format, only a few hash algorithms and truncation lengths are supported. A hash value that is truncated to 120 bits will result in the overall name being a 128-bit value, which may be useful for protocols that can easily use 128-bit identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: For protocols that want a short fixed-size name, there is a binary form: two bits of reserved space, six bits naming the hash, and the hash itself. With a 120-bit hash the whole name is 128 bits.

sections.title: The Human-Speakable nih URI Format
sections.content:
Sometimes a resource has to be referred to by a name that is easy for humans to read out and less likely to be ambiguous when heard. This is intended to be usable, for example, over the phone in order to confirm the presence or absence of a resource, and that confirmation use case is the main current use case for Named Information for Humans, or nih, URIs. The ni URI format is not well suited to this, since base64url uses both uppercase and lowercase, which can easily cause confusion. For speaking the value of a hash output, the more verbose but less ambiguous nih URI scheme is defined.

Fields in nih URIs are separated by a semicolon. The first field is a hash algorithm string, as in the ni URI format. The hash value is represented using lowercase ASCII hex characters, so an octet with the decimal value 58, 0x3A, is encoded as '3a'. This is the same as base16 encoding except that lowercase letters are used. Separator '-' characters MAY be interspersed in the hash value in any way to make it easier to read, typically grouping four or six characters with a separator between them.

The hash value MAY be followed by a semicolon and then a checkdigit. The checkdigit MUST be calculated using Luhn's mod N algorithm with N=16. The input to the calculation is the ASCII hex-encoded hash value with all '-' separator characters first stripped out, which maps '0' to 0 through '9' to 9, and 'a' to 10 through 'f' to 15. None of the other fields, nor any '-' separators, are input when calculating the checkdigit. For algorithms that have a Suite ID reserved, the alg field MAY contain the ID value as an ASCII-encoded decimal number instead of the hash name string, for example '3' instead of 'sha-256-120', and implementations MUST be able to match the decimal ID values for the algorithms and hash lengths they support, even if they do not support the binary format. There is no such thing as a relative nih URI.
sections.plainLanguage: The nih form writes the hash in lowercase hex digits, grouped with dashes, and adds one extra character that catches reading errors. It is longer than the ni form but it survives being spoken aloud.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
No secret information is required to generate or verify a name of this form, so such a name can only provide evidence for the integrity of the referenced object, and the proof of integrity is only as good as the proof of integrity for the name from which it started. The hash value provides a name-data integrity binding between the name and the bytes returned when the name is dereferenced.

Disclosure of a name value does not necessarily entail disclosure of the referenced object, but it may enable an attacker to determine the contents of the referenced object by reference to a search engine or other data repository, or for a highly formatted object with little variation, by simply guessing the value and checking whether the digest matches. The fact that these names contain hashes does not protect the confidentiality of the object that was input to the hash.

The integrity of the referenced content would be compromised if a weak hash function were used, and SHA-256 is the preferred hash algorithm, which is why only SHA-256-based suites were added to the initial IANA registry. If a truncated hash value is used, certain security properties are affected. A hash algorithm is designed to produce sufficient bits to prevent a collision from a birthday attack, and ensuring that discovering two pieces of content which result in the same digest by brute force requires a work factor of O(2^x) requires a digest length of 2x. Many security applications only require protection against a second pre-image attack, which requires a digest length of x to achieve the same work factor. The shorter the hash value used, the less security benefit can be got.

An important point is not to make the mistake of thinking two names are the same when they are not. A name with a 32-bit truncated sha-256 hash is not the same as a name with the full 256 bits of hash output, even if the hash value for one is a prefix of the other. If an application treated these as the same name, that might open up attacks: if an object is published with the full hash, an application should not treat a name with just the first 32 bits of that hash as referring to the same thing, since the 32-bit name will have many colliding objects. For that reason, the algorithm, length and value must all match before two names are considered the same.

The fact that an ni URI includes a domain name in the authority field implies nothing about the relationship between the owner of the domain name and any content referenced by that URI. There is nothing to stop anyone creating an ni URI containing a hash of someone else's content, and application developers MUST NOT assume any relationship between the registrant of the domain name and some matching content just because the ni URI matches that content. If name-data integrity is successfully validated and the hash is strong and long enough, the web origin for the bytes of the named object is the place from which the name is obtained rather than the place from which the bytes are obtained, which may be a benefit when ni names are used for scripts included from an HTML page served over authenticated https. If name-data integrity is not validated, or fails, the web origin is, as usual, the place from which the object bytes were received. Applications using ni names SHOULD take this into account in their trust models. Some implementations might mishandle ni URIs that include non-base64 characters, whitespace or other non-conforming strings, and that could lead to erroneously considering names to be the same when they are not, so an ni URI that is malformed in such ways MUST NOT be treated as matching any other ni URI.
sections.plainLanguage: A hash name proves that the bytes you fetched are the ones the name was built from. It does not prove who owns the content, and it does not keep the content secret: someone who has the name can look it up or guess it.

viz.caption: THE FIVE WAYS TO WRITE ONE NAME (RFC 6920)

items.title: ni URI
items.text: A URI of the form ni:///sha-256;f4OxZX_x_FO5LcGBSKHWXfwtSx-j1ncoSt3SABJtkGk, naming the object by hash.

items.title: .well-known URL
items.text: The same name as an HTTP address under /.well-known/ni/, for clients that do not know the ni scheme.

items.title: URL segment
items.text: The alg-val pair dropped into the pathname, query string or fragment of an ordinary HTTP URL.

items.title: Binary format
items.text: A reserved field, a Suite ID and the hash value, for protocols that need a compact fixed-size name.

items.title: nih URI
items.text: A human-speakable form that uses lowercase hex digits and a check digit, meant to be read out loud.

data.title: ni URI syntax
data.code:
NI-URI         = ni-scheme ":" ni-hier-part [ "?" query ]
    ; adapted from "URI" in RFC 3986
    ; query is from RFC 3986, Section 3.4
ni-scheme      = "ni"
ni-hier-part   = "//" [ authority ] "/" alg-val
    ; authority is from RFC 3986, Section 3.2
alg-val        = alg ";" val
    ; adapted from "hier-part" in RFC 3986
alg            = 1*unreserved
val            = 1*unreserved
    ; unreserved is from RFC 3986, Section 2.3

fields.name: Res
fields.desc: Reserved for future use. MUST be set to zero for this specification and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Suite ID
fields.desc: Specifies the hash algorithm and the truncation length.

fields.name: Hash Value
fields.desc: A possibly truncated result of a one-way hash over whatever is being identified.
